summary: A 1976 interim revision of Appendix F of BBN Report 1822, the document describing the interface between hosts and IMPs. It is a short update to that appendix.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 716 clarifies how the software layers of a Very Distant Host connection should handle packet order. It recommends waiting before retransmission to avoid unnecessary repeats when an acknowledgement is delayed.

questions: why can very distant host packets arrive out of order
when should an unacknowledged packet be retransmitted
what does rfc 716 change in report 1822
subtitle: An interim clarification of message ordering and retransmission for a Very Distant Host interface.

tldr.problem: Operators were uncertain how to handle ordering and retransmission between the software layers of a Very Distant Host interface.
tldr.mechanism: The update says packets can arrive out of order between the RTP layers and recommends an adjustable delay before retransmitting an unacknowledged packet.
tldr.outcome: The memo provides an interim revision to Appendix F of BBN Report 1822 while that report awaits revision.

today: RFC 716 is an interim logical update to Appendix F of BBN Report 1822. Its introduction says further information was intended for a later revision of that report.

sections.title: Ordering Between RTP Layers
sections.content:
A standard Host-to-IMP interface delivers and receives messages in order. In a Very Distant Host interface, the packets passed from the IMP to its RTP may be ordered, but no ordering guarantee applies between the two RTP software interfaces.

If a receiver discards an erroneous packet, a later packet may arrive on another logical channel before the sender retransmits the missing one. The receiving RTP must be prepared for that order.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets can reach the receiving software out of order even when each side handles its own channels in sequence. The receiver must allow for that case.

sections.title: Retransmission Delay
sections.content:
The memo recommends an adjustable program delay before retransmitting a packet that has not been acknowledged. It gives 100 milliseconds as a trial value, because acknowledgements may be delayed by processing and transmission.

If a later packet has been acknowledged but an earlier one has not, the earlier packet can be retransmitted immediately. The memo says this optimization had not been implemented in the IMP at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: Waiting briefly can prevent a delayed acknowledgement from causing an unnecessary repeat. If a later packet is acknowledged first, the sender already knows the earlier packet needs retransmission.

sections.title: Maintaining Channel Sequence
sections.content:
The transmitting RTP fills its logical channels in sequence, and the receiving RTP empties them in sequence. After initialization, the first channel used must be channel zero.

Null packets use no channel or channel number and are not acknowledged when received.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side follows its own channel order so the data can be put back into sequence. Null packets do not use a channel and do not receive acknowledgements.
